name: Hammurabi
summary: Sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE), he turned a small city-state into an empire covering most of Mesopotamia through diplomacy and war against Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. Late in his reign he set up stone stelae carrying 282 laws, framed as given by the sun god Shamash, so that 'the strong may not oppress the weak'. His letters show a king closely involved in canals, taxes and court cases.

summary: Daughter of Thutmose I, Hatshepsut ruled first as regent for her stepson Thutmose III and then as pharaoh (c. 1479–1458 BCE), depicted with the royal false beard. name: Cleopatra
summary: Cleopatra VII Philopator (69–30 BCE) was the last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and the only member of her Macedonian Greek dynasty to learn Egyptian; Plutarch says she spoke about nine languages. Driven from power by her brother Ptolemy XIII, she allied with Julius Caesar, who restored her to the throne in 47 BCE; she bore him a son, Caesarion. After Caesar's murder she allied with Mark Antony, bearing three children and ruling the eastern Mediterranean with him. Octavian declared war on her, and after defeat at Actium (31 BCE) both she and Antony took their own lives in Alexandria in 30 BCE — tradition says by the bite of an asp — and Egypt became a Roman province. Roman propaganda painted her as a seductress, but ancient sources also show a shrewd, educated ruler who kept Egypt independent for two decades.

name: Kanishka
summary: Kanishka I (reigned about 127–150 CE) was the greatest ruler of the Kushan Empire, descended from Yuezhi nomads who had migrated from China's frontier to Bactria. His realm stretched from Central Asia and Afghanistan to the Ganga plain, with capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, controlling key Silk Road routes. The Rabatak inscription, found in Afghanistan in 1993, lists his conquests and shows that he used Bactrian rather than Greek on his coins. He is remembered in Buddhist tradition for convening the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir and building a giant stupa at Peshawar, though his coins also show Greek, Persian and Hindu gods like Shiva, Mithra and Helios. His reign saw the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art produce some of the first images of the Buddha in human form.

name: Samudragupta
summary: Samudragupta (reigned about 335–375 CE), son of Chandragupta I and the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi, built the Gupta Empire through conquest. The Allahabad Pillar inscription, composed by his court poet Harishena on an Ashokan pillar, lists the kings he 'violently uprooted' in the Ganga valley, the southern rulers he defeated and then reinstated as tributaries, and frontier states and forest kingdoms that paid homage. He performed the ashvamedha horse sacrifice to proclaim universal sovereignty. His gold coins show him playing the veena, and the inscription praises him as a poet and music lover. The historian Vincent Smith later called him 'the Napoleon of India'.

name: Justinian I
summary: Justinian I (reigned 527–565), a peasant's son from the Balkans who rose through his uncle Justin I, was the last Byzantine emperor whose first language was Latin. With his wife Theodora, a former actress who became a powerful empress, he survived the Nika riots of 532, which nearly toppled him and burned much of Constantinople; Theodora reportedly declared that 'royalty is a good burial shroud'. He rebuilt the city, including Hagia Sophia (537), and his generals Belisarius and Narses reconquered North Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Ostrogoths. His Corpus Juris Civilis codified Roman law and later shaped European legal systems. His reign was also struck by the Plague of Justinian (541), which he survived, and his wars drained the empire.

name: Harsha
summary: Harshavardhana (reigned 606–647) of the Pushyabhuti family of Thanesar took power at 16 after his elder brother was murdered and his sister Rajyashri's husband was killed. He moved his capital to Kannauj and united much of north India. Our knowledge comes from his court poet Banabhatta's Harshacharita and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang, who described Harsha's great assemblies at Kannauj and Prayag, where every five years he gave away his treasure to monks, Brahmins and the poor. Harsha wrote three Sanskrit plays, Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika, and patronised Nalanda. His southward advance was halted by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II on the Narmada, and his empire fell apart after his death without an heir.

name: Charlemagne
summary: Charlemagne ('Charles the Great', about 747–814) became king of the Franks in 768 and spent over 30 years at war, conquering the Lombards in Italy, the Saxons (forcibly converting them, including executing 4,500 at Verden in 782), and Bavaria, and fighting in Spain, where the Battle of Roncevaux inspired the Song of Roland. On Christmas Day 800 Pope Leo III crowned him emperor in Rome. From his capital at Aachen he sponsored the Carolingian Renaissance, gathering scholars like Alcuin of York, reforming education and promoting a clear new handwriting, Carolingian minuscule, the ancestor of our lower-case letters. He exchanged embassies with the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, who sent him an elephant. His empire split among his grandsons, forming the basis of France and Germany.

name: Genghis Khan
summary: Temüjin (about 1162–1227) was born on the Mongolian steppe; after his father was poisoned, his family was abandoned and he survived poverty, captivity and the kidnapping of his wife Börte. Through alliances, loyalty-based promotion and ruthless warfare he united the Mongol and Turkic tribes, and in 1206 an assembly proclaimed him Genghis Khan ('universal ruler'). He organised his army in units of tens, hundreds and thousands, created the Yassa law code, a postal relay system and a script for Mongolian, and allowed religious freedom. His campaigns conquered northern China's Jin and Xi Xia and destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire, with massacres at cities like Nishapur and Merv. He died in 1227, and his sons and grandsons built the largest contiguous land empire in history.

summary: Razia (r. 1236–1240), daughter of Iltutmish, was named heir by her father ahead of her brothers. name: Babur
summary: Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur (1483–1530) was descended from Timur on his father's side and Genghis Khan on his mother's. He became ruler of Fergana at 11, repeatedly won and lost Samarkand, and seized Kabul in 1504. Invited by disaffected Afghan nobles, he invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 using matchlocks, field guns and flanking cavalry, then defeated Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). He founded the Mughal Empire but ruled only four years. His memoir, the Baburnama, written in Chagatai Turkic, is remarkably candid, describing battles, gardens, fruits and his homesickness for Kabul, where he asked to be buried.

name: Akbar
summary: Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar (1542–1605) became emperor at 13 after his father Humayun's death, with Bairam Khan as regent; his army won the Second Battle of Panipat (1556). He expanded the empire across north and central India, Gujarat, Bengal and Kashmir, and built a system of mansabdars (ranked officials) and a land revenue system with his finance minister Raja Todar Mal. He married Rajput princesses, appointed Hindus to high office, abolished the jizya tax and pilgrim tax, and held debates among Hindus, Muslims, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits in his Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri. His idea of sulh-i-kul ('peace with all') and his short-lived Din-i Ilahi reflected religious tolerance. Though illiterate, he patronised the 'nine jewels' of his court, including Tansen and Birbal, and Abul Fazl wrote his history, the Akbarnama.

name: Sargon of Akkad

A later legend says he was born to a priestess who set him adrift in a reed basket on the Euphrates, and he was raised by a gardener; he rose to be cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish. He seized power, built a new capital at Akkad (whose location is still unknown), and defeated Lugalzagesi of Uruk to conquer all the Sumerian cities. He installed Akkadian governors, a standing army of 5,400 men, and trade links reaching Meluhha (the Indus Valley). He made his daughter Enheduanna high priestess at Ur, and his dynasty ruled for about 150 years.

name: Immanuel Kant
summary: Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) spent his entire life in Königsberg, Prussia, famous for his punctual daily walks. name: Alexander Graham Bell
role: Inventor and teacher of the deaf
summary: Born in Edinburgh to a family of speech teachers — his mother and wife were deaf — Bell emigrated to Canada and then Boston, where he taught deaf students.
